# The Best Laptops for College Students

Laptops for college should be portable, offer long battery life, and be well priced. Based on testing hundreds of laptops, these are my top picks.

Courtesy of Apple

College laptops don’t have to be embarrassing. Nor do they have to be overly expensive. There are a lot of great, well-designed laptops for college students that combine long battery life, easy portability, and the performance needed for everyday coursework.

In my decade-plus of reviewing laptops, I’ve tested hundreds of models. If someone asked me what to buy for a college student, these are the ones I’d suggest.

Be sure to check out our other computing guides, including the Best Laptops, Best Budget Laptops, Best MacBooks, Best Windows Laptops, Best Gaming Laptops, Best Chromebooks, and Best Laptop Bags.

Updated July 2026: I’ve added the HP OmniBook 3 and Dell 14 Plus as picks, and the Dell 14S as an honorable mention. I’ve also removed some options that have become too expensive after price increases.

## The Best Overall College Laptop

- Photograph: Luke Larsen
- Photograph: Luke Larsen
- Photograph: Luke Larsen
- Photograph: Luke Larsen

Apple

### MacBook Neo

Apple

The MacBook Air (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is my choice for best overall laptop for everyone. But college students have specific needs—and often, specific budgets. In addition to being affordable, a college student’s laptop should be lightweight and easy to carry around. The MacBook Neo (7/10, WIRED Recommends) fits the bill perfectly. It’s only 2.7 pounds and starts at just $699. It also has a smaller display, which helps it fit on those tiny lecture-hall desks. What makes the MacBook Neo special, however, is its lack of compromise around quality. It’s a gorgeous piece of hardware, with fun colors, an excellent trackpad, a beautiful display, and that Apple “it” factor. I recommend the $699 model, which gets you twice the storage and a Touch ID fingerprint reader.

Of course, this isn’t a laptop without downsides. Apple invested its efforts in the front-of-screen experience, but made cuts to performance, ports, and memory to keep costs low. The limitation of 8 GB of memory is my biggest sticking point with this device; it means you’ll need to be mindful of how many applications, tabs, and background tasks you have running at once. Also, ghe Neo can connect to only one external display at a time.

Dell

### 14 Plus

Dell (512 GB)

Laptop pricing has skyrocketed over the past few months, which has made it harder to recommend some of the flashier new laptops of the year. Fortunately, many really great laptops from 2025 are still available to buy. The Dell 14 Plus is a great example. It’s one of the few laptops you can get for less than $1,000 that doesn’t force you to make serious compromises. It’s not the world’s prettiest device, but the display is surprisingly sharp, bright, and colorful. The computer’s touchpad and keyboard are both high-quality, and it has tons of ports.

The newer Dell 14S came out more recently with the intention to replace the 14 Plus. The new model comes with an OLED display and superb battery life. While it’s a solid option (see Other Laptops to Consider, below), it starts at a pricey $1,350, and the screen has a lower resolution. For a college student, the Dell 14 Plus is the better buy right now.

## A Featherlight College Laptop

Asus

### Zenbook A14

If the idea of buying a laptop with only 8 GB of RAM in 2026 seems questionable (I don’t blame you for feeling this way), I recommend the Asus Zenbook A14 (WIRED Recommends, 8/10). Not only does it come with 16 GB of RAM, but it’s the lightest laptop you can buy right now at just 2.4 pounds. You’ll hardly notice it in your laptop bag when you’re trekking across campus.

The price of the Zenbook A14 varies quite a bit, typically between $600 and $1,000, but there’s often a deal available that makes it an affordable option. There’s also the 2026 model, which comes with the second-gen Snapdragon X2 chip. At $1,600, though, it’s just not worth the extra cash—especially for a college student on a budget.

## The Best Cheap College Laptop

HP

### OmniBook 5

The options listed above are fairly affordable, all coming in at less than $1,000. But even if your budget is $600 or less, trust that you can still get a solidly performing laptop with good battery life. The HP OmniBook 5 frequently sells for around $600 or less, making it an adequate MacBook Neo alternative. Better yet, HP’s laptop ships with more memory and storage. The OLED panel display is fantastic too, and the laptop is remarkably thin. The only significant downside is the touchpad, which feels clumsy to use. I could get used to it over time, but it is the Achilles’ heel of this OmniBook 5 (and nearly all budget laptops, for that matter).

- Photograph: Luke Larsen
- Photograph: Luke Larsen
- Photograph: Luke Larsen

HP

### OmniBook 3 (2026)

If you need a super-cheap Windows laptop, though, there’s really only one I’d recommend that’s cheaper than the OmniBook 5, and it comes from the same family. I tested the HP OmniBook 3 and found that it shares a lot of the positive qualities of its older sibling. The OLED screen is great, as is the keyboard and overall build quality. Most important, the battery life is top-notch for a device of this price. It’s not as thin as the OmniBook 5 though, and the 1920 x 1200 resolution stretched across the 16-inch screen is unfortunate. There’s also a 14-inch version, which I think is a smarter buy.

But there’s not a single other Windows laptop I’d feel good about suggesting someone buy at this price. Intel-powered laptops at this price tend to struggle with performance and battery life, while other cheap Qualcomm Snapdragon X laptops like the Asus Vivobook 14 use terrible displays to drag the prices down.

## The Best College Laptop Under $500

### Chromebook CX15

Chromebooks are becoming increasingly tough to sell. Snapdragon X-powered laptops like the HP OmniBook 3 above have made budget-tier Chromebooks, with weak battery life and poor screens, harder to justify. Furthermore, Chromebooks have the added problem of incompatibility with certain software you might need in college.

However, Chromebooks are still the way to go if you need something— anything—for as little money as possible. If you’re low on cash and just need basic internet access, the $200 Asus Chromebook CX15 is your best bet. The screen and touchpad are the main downfalls, but it’s fairly portable and modern-looking, and the battery life is decent enough. My bar is fairly low for a $200 laptop, but the CX15 outdoes other competitors at this price.

## Best Powerful College Laptops for STEM

### LOQ 15

Lenovo (RTX 5050, 512 GB)

Not everyone needs a powerful laptop to tote around campus. But if you’re in a STEM field, or even just like to play games on the weekend, buying a single, powerful laptop to serve as your main machine at college is a good idea. Unfortunately, no gaming laptop is powerful, portable, and affordable—you can only have two of those three things. Letting go of the portability priority, the best option I’ve tested is the Lenovo LOQ 15 (8/10, WIRED Recommends). It’s hard to beat a discrete graphics processing unit (GPU) for raw performance, which is exactly what the RTX 5060 in the LOQ 15 delivers. Though the price often creeps above $1,000, it’s still the most affordable gaming laptop you can buy that doesn’t suffer from severe performance compromises.

### Blade 16 (2025)

Razer

Now, if you can afford to dish out some more money, I’d point you to either the Razer Blade 16 or the MacBook Pro. Despite the thin profile of the Razer Blade 16 (8/10 WIRED Recommends), you can configure it with up to an RTX 5090 graphics card. Aside from the compromise of a high price, battery life is a limitation. You might run out halfway through your day, forcing you to find an outlet in a hurry. If you happen to need performance for gaming on the weekends in addition to your schoolwork, the Razer Blade 16 is expensive but totally worth it. I prefer the smaller Razer Blade 14 as a college laptop, but it’s no longer available to purchase right now.

The MacBook Pro, whether you opt for the M5 Pro, M5 Max, or an older chip, resolves the issue of battery life. Gaming isn’t its strongest capability, but it delivers exceptional performance in creative applications and can be equipped with up to 128 GB of unified memory for serious on-device AI workloads.

## Other Laptops to Consider for College

Photograph: Luke Larsen

Dell 14S for $1,350: While this laptop is more expensive than I’d like, it’s a solid choice. The chassis is more polished than that of the Dell 14 Plus, and the glossy OLED screen gives the device a premium look. I wish it were brighter, or at least handled glare better.

MacBook Air for $1,260: In previous years, the MacBook Air has been my top pick for college laptops, but in 2026, the prices and available configurations have gone up considerably. While it’s still overall the best laptop you can buy, the MacBook Neo is a better option for most college students, given its lower price.

Photograph: Luke Larsen

Apple iPad Air for $899: iPads can be solid laptop replacements, as long as you get the right one. The latest M4 iPad Air (7/10, WIRED Recommends) is the best example, as it’s not too expensive but still gives you the option of a larger, 13-inch display. The recent changes to iPadOS bring desktop-like multitasking to the platform, and when paired with a Magic Keyboard, you get a very capable 2-in-1 laptop. It’s an expensive accessory, but the keyboard and trackpad are both top-notch, on par with a high-end laptop.

Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x for $1,075: When it launched, this well-rounded, 15-inch laptop was selling for just $850. These days, it’s a few hundred dollars more, which is why I dropped it from a top pick to an honorable mention. The screen is brighter and more colorful than I expected, and even the touchpad feels smooth and responsive. It even gets excellent battery life and delivers a good balance between screen size and portability.

Microsoft Surface Pro 12

Photograph: Luke Larsen

Microsoft Surface Pro 12 for $750: I can’t think of a better device to bring to class for note-taking than the Surface Pro 12 (6/10, WIRED Recommends). While I recommend the larger Surface Pro 13 for most people, college students are the exception. The thinner and lighter size of the Surface Pro 12 gives you a super-portable Windows device. It has really solid hardware too. The Snapdragon X Plus provides just as much power and long-lasting battery life as the larger model. I wish it were a bit more affordable, as you’ll still need to add on the Surface keyboard and a USB-C power supply.

Framework Laptop 12 for $549: You can’t expect most budget laptops to last longer than four years of college. The Framework Laptop 12 (7/10, WIRED Recommends) promises something longer-lasting, as all Framework laptops do. This one is the smallest and cheapest in the lineup, and despite the price, the display and trackpad are both better than I expected. The only problem is the limited RAM.

Yes. Or, at the very least, some type of computing device you’re comfortable using. A laptop is still the preferred recommendation, but you could alternatively use a desktop in your dorm room paired with an iPad or a note-taking device in class.

The mobile aspect of a laptop makes it extremely easy to take your work with you between classes, while studying in coffee shops or typing notes in lecture, for example. Additionally, a laptop makes it easy to save space in cramped dorm rooms.

But as seen in my recommendations above, devices like the iPad Air and Surface Pro 12 could also be good solutions, as long as you pair them with their respective keyboard accessories.

All our guidelines for choosing a laptop also apply to college laptops, including evaluating the quality of the display and chassis, along with ensuring that the device is fast enough for your work. There are, however, a couple of important considerations specific to college. Portability and battery life are paramount. Regardless of your budget, you want something that will last throughout the day and won't weigh you down while you carry it from class to class. Anything more than 4 pounds will start to feel noticeable in your backpack.

Overall dimensions are important, too. Bringing a 16-inch laptop to class can feel obtuse, given the size of small desks. The same is true if you plan on bringing your laptop to a crowded coffee shop or library. That’s why 13- or 14-inch laptops are preferred. There are even 14-inch gaming laptops, such as the Razer Blade 14, that provide the discrete GPU performance you need without sacrificing portability.

Here are some other specs to consider:

Processor

- Windows: If you’re getting a Windows machine, your main options for the processor are Intel or Qualcomm. Both have strengths and weaknesses, but getting a Snapdragon X laptop ensures that you get really solid battery life. See our full guide to buying a laptop for more info.
- Chromebooks: These browser-based machines use half a dozen processors, most of which you’ve probably never heard of. There’s a reason for that: Those processors are slow. My recommendation when buying a Chromebook is to stick with a Chromebook Plus machine. This is a new standard Google created to ensure a certain level of performance and polish.
- MacOS: Apple has been making its own processors for a few years, like the latest M5 chip found inside the latest MacBook Pro. These more powerful MacBook Pros feature integrated GPUs that aim to be comparable with the discrete GPUs you find in Windows laptops. Our MacBook buying guide can help further.

RAM and Storage

Regardless of which OS you choose, the minimum amount of RAM you want in your laptop is 8 GB. That’s enough memory to keep your computer feeling snappy even if it’s running under load. But these days 16 GB is standard, and you’ll find lots of laptops around $800 or less that come with 16 GB. So, if you can afford it—especially if you plan to edit photos or videos as part of your coursework—go for a 16-GB or even 32-GB model.

The new default for storage is 256 GB, and it’ll do if you’re trying to save money. You can always use external storage if you need to add on. Spring for 512 GB or a terabyte if you can, though.

Screen

Screens vary tremendously, but don’t settle for anything less than 1080p (or 1200p for 16:10 aspect ratio displays). For a 13-inch laptop, 1080p is sharp enough. If you’re going with a bigger laptop, 2.5K or even 4K screens will improve the viewing experience. If you’re trying to play games as well, be sure to get something with a higher refresh rate— 120 Hz or 144 Hz will more than satisfy.

Weight and Battery

Don’t forget you’ll be lugging this thing around. It may be tugging on your back for eight hours or more. At the end of a long day of walking, you will likely notice the difference between a 3-pound and 4-pound laptop. Trust me. Also, consider picking out a nice bag to carry your computer in.

Similarly, battery life is very important when you’re (potentially) away from a wall outlet for extended periods. Whatever you end up getting, make sure it’s capable of lasting at least eight hours under real-world use—browsing the web, editing documents, writing emails, and taking notes. Even then, you might want to consider a portable battery charger.

Yes, for most college students, Chromebooks are a good option. They are cheaper than MacBooks or Windows laptops, and the Chromebook Plus models offer reliable performance at an affordable price. If your budget is $500 or less, things can get more iffy, but I’ve tested a couple of good options that I recommend in this guide in that price range.

Furthermore, you can run almost all apps in the web these days (including Office 365), and Android apps do a good job of filling in the gaps. Occasionally, though, you may run into some compatibility problems, whether with software or hardware. If you’re in a STEM, art, or design program, however, a Chromebook is probably not a good fit. For example, if you’re required to use CAD or Photoshop, you’ll want a Windows laptop.

# Best Laptops for Computer Science Students 2026: Coding, CS Degree and Programming Picks

 July 15, 2026 June 17, 2026 by T Karlilar 

Choosing the best laptop for computer science students in 2026 depends on what kind of coursework, coding projects, and technical tools you expect to use. A first-year student learning Python, Java, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, or basic databases does not need the same laptop as someone running Android Studio, virtual machines, Linux tools, Docker alternatives, cybersecurity labs, data projects, and multiple browser tabs at the same time.

For many computer science students, a good laptop should be portable, reliable, comfortable to type on, and powerful enough to last through several years of study. You do not always need the most expensive machine, but you should avoid very weak laptops with low RAM, slow storage, poor screens, or uncomfortable keyboards.

This guide compares the best laptops for computer science students, coding classes, programming assignments, software engineering projects, data structures, web development, app development, cybersecurity study, virtual machines, and general student productivity in 2026.

## Quick Verdict

Best overall laptop for computer science students: MacBook Air M5

Best Windows laptop for CS students: Lenovo ThinkPad T14 Gen 6

Best laptop for heavier CS labs and VMs: ThinkPad P14s Gen 6

Best premium Mac for CS students: MacBook Pro 14

Best portable value-style pick: ASUS Zenbook 14

Best sleek Windows laptop for students: Dell XPS 13

If you want a simple, portable, long-lasting laptop for coding and student life, the MacBook Air M5 is the easiest overall pick for many students. If your course requires Windows software, Linux flexibility, virtual machines, or business-style reliability, the ThinkPad T14 Gen 6 is the safer Windows choice. If your workload is heavier, the ThinkPad P14s Gen 6 gives you more technical headroom.

## Best Laptops for Computer Science Students Compared

| Laptop | Best For | Main Strength | Main Weakness |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MacBook Air M5 | Most CS students who want portability and battery life | Lightweight, quiet, strong battery life, macOS coding workflow | Not ideal for every Windows-only course requirement |
| Lenovo ThinkPad T14 Gen 6 | Windows, Linux learning, coding, and serious student work | Keyboard, reliability, business design, and strong RAM options | Less sleek than lifestyle ultrabooks |
| ThinkPad P14s Gen 6 | Virtual machines, cybersecurity labs, and heavier CS projects | Workstation-style ThinkPad option | Can cost more depending on configuration |
| MacBook Pro 14 | Premium Mac users and heavier development work | Performance, display, battery life, premium build | Usually expensive for students |
| ASUS Zenbook 14 | Students who want a portable, premium-feeling Windows laptop | Display options, portability, and good value depending on the deal | Not as business-focused as ThinkPad |
| Dell XPS 13 | Students who want a compact premium Windows laptop | Sleek design and portability | Port setup and keyboard feel may not suit everyone |

## 1. MacBook Air M5: Best Overall Laptop for Computer Science Students

The MacBook Air M5 is the best overall pick for many computer science students because it combines portability, battery life, quiet operation, strong everyday performance, and a clean macOS development environment. It is easy to carry around campus, comfortable for lectures, and strong enough for coding, research, web development, documents, notes, video calls, and general student use.

For computer science students who work with Python, JavaScript, web development, Git, VS Code, terminals, browser tabs, documentation, and general programming assignments, the MacBook Air M5 can be an excellent choice. It is also a good fit if you already use an iPhone, iPad, AirPods, iCloud, or other Apple devices.

The main warning is course compatibility. Some computer science courses, engineering tools, cybersecurity labs, or Windows-only applications may be easier on a Windows laptop. Before buying a Mac, check your university’s software requirements and ask whether Windows is required for any modules.

If your course is mostly coding, web development, Python, Java, databases, and general software work, the MacBook Air M5 is one of the easiest laptops to recommend. If you expect heavy virtual machines or Windows-specific tools, consider the ThinkPad T14 or ThinkPad P14s instead.

For another Apple comparison, read our ThinkPad T14 Gen 6 vs MacBook Air M5 vs Dell XPS 13 comparison.

## 2. Lenovo ThinkPad T14 Gen 6: Best Windows Laptop for CS Students

The Lenovo ThinkPad T14 Gen 6 is the best Windows laptop here for computer science students who want a practical, reliable, work-focused machine for coding, Linux learning, virtual machines, documentation, browser tabs, and long study sessions.

For CS students, the keyboard is a serious advantage. You may spend hours writing code, debugging, taking notes, writing reports, using terminals, searching documentation, and switching between lectures, assignments, and browser tabs. A comfortable keyboard can matter more than a slightly thinner design.

The ThinkPad T14 Gen 6 is especially useful if your course involves Windows tools, Linux environments, virtual machines, databases, cybersecurity labs, Microsoft software, remote desktops, or business-style development workflows.

A 16GB RAM configuration can work for many students, but 32GB RAM is the better long-term choice if you plan to run virtual machines, Android Studio, local databases, multiple IDEs, many browser tabs, or heavier final-year projects.

Read our full Lenovo ThinkPad T14 Gen 6 review.

## 3. ThinkPad P14s Gen 6: Best for Heavier CS Labs and Virtual Machines

The ThinkPad P14s Gen 6 is the best choice here for computer science students who expect heavier workloads. It makes sense if your course includes virtual machines, cybersecurity labs, software testing environments, data projects, engineering tools, technical research, or larger programming projects.

Compared with a normal student laptop, the ThinkPad P14s feels more like a compact workstation-style machine. That can be useful if your laptop needs to run a host operating system, Linux VMs, Windows test machines, code editors, browsers, terminals, databases, and notes at the same time.

This laptop is not necessary for every first-year student. If you are mostly doing basic programming and web development, the MacBook Air, ThinkPad T14, Zenbook 14, or Dell XPS 13 may be enough. But if you want more headroom for technical labs, the ThinkPad P14s Gen 6 is the strongest pick in this guide.

For this kind of student workload, 32GB RAM and a 1TB SSD are strongly worth considering. Virtual machine files, SDKs, project folders, course material, datasets, and snapshots can use storage quickly.

If your workload includes VMs, read our guide to the best laptops for virtual machines and VMware in 2026.

## 4. MacBook Pro 14: Best Premium Mac for Computer Science Students

The MacBook Pro 14 is the best premium Mac option for computer science students who want more performance, a better display, stronger sustained workloads, and a more professional laptop than the MacBook Air.

It makes sense for students who do heavier development work, app development, creative coding, data projects, multitasking, external monitor use, video work, or long coding sessions. It can also be a good fit for students who want one laptop for university and professional work after graduation.

The downside is price. Many computer science students do not need a MacBook Pro 14. If your coursework is mostly basic programming, lectures, documents, browser tabs, and light projects, the MacBook Air M5 may be the smarter Apple choice.

The MacBook Pro 14 becomes easier to justify if you know you want macOS, stronger performance, a better screen, more memory, and a laptop that can handle heavier work for several years.

For coding-focused comparisons, read our guide to the best laptops for programming and coding in 2026.

## 5. ASUS Zenbook 14: Best Portable Value-Style Pick

The ASUS Zenbook 14 is a good option for computer science students who want a portable Windows laptop with a premium feel, strong display options, and good everyday performance without jumping straight to expensive business or workstation pricing.

For CS students, the Zenbook 14 can make sense for coding, web development, Python practice, SQL learning, online courses, documents, browser tabs, video calls, and general university work. It is also easier to carry than many larger laptops.

The Zenbook 14 is not the most corporate or workstation-style laptop here, so it may not be the best choice for heavy virtual machines, long cybersecurity labs, or demanding technical workloads. But for many students, it can be a good balance of portability, comfort, and value.

Choose the strongest configuration you can reasonably afford. For computer science, 16GB RAM should be treated as the sensible minimum, while 32GB RAM is better for heavier multitasking or virtual machine work.

For more portable choices, read our guide to the best lightweight laptops for work in 2026.

## 6. Dell XPS 13: Best Sleek Windows Laptop for CS Students

The Dell XPS 13 is a good choice if you want a sleek, compact Windows laptop for computer science, coding, notes, research, web development, and student productivity. It is especially appealing if you want a premium-feeling Windows machine that is easy to carry.

For CS students, the XPS 13 can handle code editors, browser tabs, terminals, meetings, documents, and general development work depending on the configuration. It is a more stylish option than a traditional business laptop.

The trade-off is practicality. Some students may prefer the keyboard, ports, and business-style layout of a ThinkPad. If you use external monitors, USB accessories, Ethernet adapters, or lab hardware, check your docking setup before buying a very compact laptop.

The Dell XPS 13 is best for students who value portability, design, and Windows compatibility, but do not need a workstation-style machine.

## What Specs Matter for Computer Science Students?

For computer science students, the most important specs are RAM, processor performance, SSD storage, keyboard comfort, screen quality, battery life, portability, and operating system compatibility.

For basic programming and first-year coding, 16GB RAM is a sensible minimum. For heavier coursework, Android Studio, virtual machines, local databases, cybersecurity labs, data projects, Docker-style workflows, or many browser tabs, 32GB RAM is a better long-term choice.

Storage matters too. A 512GB SSD can work for many students, but 1TB is safer if you keep virtual machines, SDKs, datasets, projects, course videos, notes, backups, and large development environments on the laptop.

Keyboard comfort is easy to underestimate. Computer science students type constantly, so a good keyboard can make daily coding and note-taking much more comfortable.

Students who want to learn hardware upgrades while using Windows or Linux should consider our Framework Laptop 13 review.

## Windows, macOS, or Linux for Computer Science?

There is no single best operating system for every computer science student. The safest answer is to check your university or course requirements before buying.

macOS is popular for coding, web development, terminals, Unix-like workflows, Python, JavaScript, and general student productivity. Windows is safer if your course requires Windows software, Microsoft tools, Visual Studio, business applications, or easier compatibility with some lab environments. Linux is excellent for learning operating systems, servers, development tools, and open-source workflows, but it may require more setup as a main student laptop.

Many students are best served by Windows or macOS as the main system, then using Linux through virtual machines, WSL, cloud labs, or dual boot only when needed.

If your coursework also includes CAD, MATLAB, engineering software, simulations, or design projects, also read our guide to the best laptops for engineering students in 2026. If you are comparing student laptops for architecture, CAD, 3D modeling, or design software instead of pure coding, also read our guide to the best laptops for architecture students in 2026. 

Computer science students studying numerical computing, algorithms, data processing or scientific programming should also see our guide to the best laptops for MATLAB in 2026. Students specializing in databases or backend development should also compare our recommended SQL development laptops. Students specialising in networking, infrastructure or Cisco certifications should compare our best laptops for network engineering.

## Do Computer Science Students Need 32GB RAM?

Not always. If you are learning basic programming, web development, Java, Python, SQL, algorithms, or data structures, 16GB RAM is usually enough.

However, 32GB RAM becomes much more useful if you run Android Studio, virtual machines, Linux labs, cybersecurity tools, local databases, large IDEs, many browser tabs, or heavier final-year projects.

If memory is your main concern, read our guide to the best laptops with 32GB RAM for work in 2026.

Students building 2D, 3D or mobile games can compare dedicated development systems in our Unity laptop guide.

## Final Verdict

The best laptop for computer science students in 2026 depends on your course requirements, budget, operating system preference, and how heavy your coding workload will become.

Choose the MacBook Air M5 if you want the easiest overall laptop for coding, portability, battery life, notes, lectures, and general student use.

Choose the Lenovo ThinkPad T14 Gen 6 if you want the safest Windows laptop for computer science, coding, Linux learning, virtual machines, and serious productivity.

Choose the ThinkPad P14s Gen 6 if you expect heavier CS labs, virtual machines, cybersecurity work, software testing, or technical projects.

Choose the MacBook Pro 14 if you want a premium Mac with stronger performance and a better screen than the MacBook Air.

Choose the ASUS Zenbook 14 if you want a portable, premium-feeling Windows laptop with good value, depending on the deal.

Choose the Dell XPS 13 if you want a sleek, compact Windows laptop for coding and student productivity.

If your main focus is coding, read our guide to the best laptops for programming and coding in 2026. If your coursework includes virtual machines, read our guide to the best laptops for virtual machines and VMware in 2026. If you are also studying cybersecurity, read our guide to the best laptops for cybersecurity and ethical hacking in 2026.

 August 24, 2026 August 24, 2026 by Burak Boğa

I’ve lost count of how many times a first-year CS student has messaged me a link to some laptop with “16GB RAM! 1TB SSD! Free Microsoft Office!” splashed across the listing, asking if it’s a good deal. Nine times out of ten it isn’t, and the reason is never the thing they’re worried about.

They worry about the processor. They should worry about whether the memory is soldered.

So here’s what I’ve done. I’ve gone through every credible lab review published on the sub-$1,000 laptops worth considering right now — Notebookcheck’s teardowns, PCWorld’s battery rundowns, Tom’s Hardware’s thermal probes, Laptop Mag’s web-surfing tests, Consumer Reports’ runtime numbers — and I’ve pulled out the measurements that actually predict whether a laptop survives a computer science degree. Not the ones that make good headlines.

Five machines made the cut. Every number below is attributed to the lab that produced it, so you can go check my work.

## The short answer

| Pick | Best for | Price right now | Why it’s here |

| Dell 14 Plus (DB14250) | Screen and battery, zero compatibility drama | $949–$995 | 2.5K 16:10 panel, Thunderbolt 4, and every x86 tool just runs. |
| Lenovo LOQ 15 (RTX 5060) | Machine learning, graphics, game dev | $799–$999 | 8GB of VRAM at a full 115 watts. Cheapest legitimate CUDA box there is. |
| HP OmniBook 5 14 | Battery life above all else | $899 | Three labs measured 25 to 32 hours. Read the ARM section first. |
| Apple MacBook Neo | Cheapest real macOS machine | $699 | Genuinely brilliant for $699. Also 8GB of RAM, permanently. |

If you take one thing from this article: buy memory, not megahertz. A 2019 laptop with 32GB is a nicer place to write code today than a 2026 laptop with 8GB. That’s not a hot take, it’s just what happens when Docker Desktop opens.

## What a CS degree actually does to a laptop

Most “best student laptops” lists are written by people who think university is Google Docs with extra steps. So let me be specific about the workload I’m judging these against, because it changes everything.

Over four years you’ll be asked to run three or four Docker containers while your IDE indexes a few hundred files in the background. You’ll spin up a Linux VM for your operating systems course and then deliberately break it. You’ll compile something genuinely large — an LLVM pass, a Rust workspace, a kernel — while a deadline ticks. You’ll boot an Android emulator, which is a virtual machine, on top of an IDE that’s already eaten 4GB before you’ve typed a character. And you’ll do a decent chunk of this in a lecture hall where every outlet within four rows was claimed twenty minutes before you arrived.

That’s the job. Three things determine whether a laptop can hold it down:

Memory, and whether you can add more later. This is the whole ballgame. 16GB is the 2026 floor and 32GB is where you want to be if containers or VMs are on your syllabus. Almost every thin-and-light sold today solders the RAM to the board, which means whatever you buy on day one is what you’re stuck with on graduation day.

Sustained performance, not burst performance. Every chip looks fast in a ten-second benchmark. What matters is what it’s doing at minute twelve of a build, once the heatsink is saturated. Thin fanless machines fall off a cliff here. Thicker ones with real fans don’t.

Battery under load, not battery playing video. Manufacturer numbers come from looping a video file at low brightness. Compiling code with fifteen tabs open and a container idling is a completely different power draw. In my experience the honest figure is roughly 40 to 60 percent of the advertised one — sometimes worse. I’ve flagged this per machine below.

Everything else — thinness, colour accuracy, the AI branding on the box — is secondary.

## How I picked these five

I don’t run a hardware lab, and I’m not going to pretend otherwise by making up numbers. What I do is read the labs that do, cross-check them against each other, and translate the results into something useful for someone writing code rather than editing video.

Here’s what I weighted, and why:

Teardown and upgrade path. Notebookcheck and iFixit-style teardowns tell you what a spec sheet won’t: how many RAM slots exist, whether there’s a second M.2 bay, whether the battery is a twenty-minute job or a nightmare. This got the heaviest weight of anything in my scoring, because it’s the single factor that decides two-year laptop versus four-year laptop.

Sustained thermal behaviour. I looked for reviews that report surface temperatures and internal temperatures during a long stress run — not just a peak number, but where the heat lands. If a laptop puts 42°C between the G and H keys, you’re going to feel it every single day.

Battery results with the test named. A 25-hour result and a 32-hour result can describe the same laptop tested two different ways. I’ve listed the test alongside the number every time so you can compare like with like.

Display brightness and coverage, measured. Manufacturer nit ratings are aspirational. Measured ones aren’t. Below 300 nits, a lecture hall with windows becomes a mirror.

Storage behaviour under sustained writes. Cheap TLC drives look fast in a ten-second benchmark and then collapse once the SLC cache fills. Which is exactly what happens when you clone a big repo or unpack a dataset. Notebookcheck specifically flags this on one of the machines below.

And then the boring stuff: keyboard quality, port selection, whether the manufacturer publishes a service manual with part numbers, and how the thing depreciates.

If you want to verify any of this on a unit you’ve bought, it takes an afternoon: Geekbench 6 three times cold, a ten-minute Cinebench loop comparing the first score against the last, CrystalDiskMark, and then a real build — `npm install` on a cold cache, a Gradle build with no daemon, a cold `docker compose up`. That last group tells you more than every synthetic benchmark combined.

## 5 Best Laptops Under $1,000 for CS Students — 2026 Buyer’s Guide

### 1. Lenovo ThinkPad E14 Gen 7 (AMD) — the one I’d actually buy

Lenovo ThinkPad E14 Gen 7 (AMD)

$780–$900 for the Ryzen 7 250 / 16GB / 512GB configuration with Windows 11 Pro

This doesn’t win on any single spec. It wins because of two DDR5 SODIMM slots and an empty M.2 2280 bay.

Every other laptop in this article solders its memory down. What you buy is what you die with. The E14 lets you buy the cheap 16GB version now and, when your distributed systems course hands you a five-container Compose file in second year, drop in an $80 kit and carry on. Lenovo rates it to 64GB and there’s a second SSD slot sitting empty next to it.

That’s not a bonus feature. That’s the difference between a laptop that gets you to graduation and one that gets you to third year.

#### The specs

- CPU: AMD Ryzen 7 250 — 8 cores, 16 threads, Zen 4, boost to 5.1GHz, 16 TOPS NPU
- Graphics: Radeon 780M integrated
- Memory: 16GB DDR5-5600 SODIMM — two slots, upgradeable to 64GB
- Storage: 512GB PCIe Gen4 NVMe — plus a free M.2 2280 PCIe 4.0 x4 slot
- Display: 14-inch WUXGA (1920×1200), IPS, anti-glare, 60Hz, 300 nits
- Ports: USB4 / Thunderbolt-class USB-C, second USB-C, USB-A 10Gbps, USB-A 5Gbps, HDMI 2.1, RJ-45 Ethernet, 3.5mm
- Wireless: Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 5.x
- OS: Windows 11 Pro — Hyper-V and BitLocker included, no upgrade fee
- Build: aluminium top and bottom covers, roughly 1.32kg, MIL-STD-810H tested
- Security: fingerprint reader in the power button, IR camera, discrete TPM 2.0
- Extras: Harman Kardon stereo speakers with Dolby Atmos, backlit keyboard

#### ⚠️ Buy the AMD one. This matters more than anything else in this section.

Lenovo sells the E14 Gen 7 with three different processor families, and they are not the same laptop inside.

Notebookcheck tore down the Lunar Lake version (Core Ultra 5 228V) and found exactly what you’d fear: Lunar Lake packages its memory on the CPU die, so there are no RAM slots at all — and Lenovo also removed the second SSD slot, leaving the space empty. The reviewer called that decision especially hard to justify, and concluded that the Arrow Lake variant, which keeps two RAM slots, is probably the better overall buy despite worse battery life.

So: the Lunar Lake E14 Gen 7 is soldered and single-drive. The AMD and Arrow Lake versions are not.

Two laptops, same model name, same picture on the retailer page, completely different lifespans. Check the processor before you check anything else. If the listing says “Core Ultra 228V” or any 200V-series chip, walk away.

#### What the performance actually looks like

Let’s be honest about the chip. The Ryzen 7 250 is a rebadged Ryzen 7 8840U — Zen 4 “Hawk Point” silicon wearing a 2026 model number. Notebookcheck confirmed this in their spec breakdowns, listing it as Hawk Point-U with a 43W sustained power limit and 53W short burst.

AMD does this a lot lately. Notebookcheck’s review of the newer Ryzen AI 7 450 landed on the same conclusion from the other direction: compared to the Ryzen AI 7 350 it replaces, performance had barely moved at all.

Does the rebadging matter for you? Less than you’d think. Eight Zen 4 cores at 5.1GHz compile perfectly well, and 16 threads beats the 8 threads you get from Lunar Lake in the Dell below. What it means practically is: don’t pay a premium for the “AI” branding on this chip. It’s a good 2024 processor with a 2026 name and it should be priced accordingly.

Where it does win is sustained load. The E14 has a proper dual-fan-free heatsink arrangement with real chassis volume to dump heat into, which means it holds boost clocks longer than any fanless ultrabook here.

#### Battery: fine, not exciting

Reviews of the Gen 7 put real-world office use — email, documents, video calls — at around 7 to 8 hours from the 48Wh cell, and that’s on the more efficient Lunar Lake configuration. Expect the AMD version to land a bit under that, and expect roughly 4 to 5 hours if you’re compiling and running containers.

It’ll get you through a day of lectures. It won’t get you through a day of lectures plus an evening in the library. Bring the charger; it’s a 65W USB-C brick, so anything decent will run it.

#### The keyboard is not a marketing point

You will type somewhere north of half a million characters getting a CS degree. The ThinkPad keyboard — proper travel, curved keycaps, an honest tactile bottom-out — is why working engineers keep buying these when their employer would happily expense something prettier. I’d tell anyone to sit down at one for ten minutes before dismissing this as brand loyalty. It’s the single most underrated spec on any laptop.

#### Pros

- Two RAM slots to 64GB. The only machine here you can rescue in year two.
- Free M.2 2280 slot. Add 2TB for around $90 instead of buying a new laptop.
- Windows 11 Pro included — Hyper-V, full WSL2, BitLocker
- Matte anti-glare panel. Lecture hall windows won’t turn it into a mirror.
- Best keyboard in the price bracket by a distance
- Actual Ethernet port, which your networking labs will thank you for
- 16 threads — more than the Lunar Lake competition for parallel builds
- Lenovo publishes a full hardware maintenance manual with part numbers. You can genuinely repair this thing.
- MIL-STD-810H tested, and it’s built like it

#### Cons

- The 300-nit, 45% NTSC display is dim and flat. Fine for code, bad for anything visual.
- Ryzen 7 250 is Zen 4 with a 2026 badge. Reviewers have been blunt about it.
- 48Wh battery is small for a 14-inch machine; 7–8 hours light use is decent, not great
- Wi-Fi 6E, not Wi-Fi 7
- 60Hz. After 120Hz, scrolling through code here feels slightly gluey.
- PC-ABS plastic base under the aluminium covers — it’s the accessible ThinkPad, not the premium one
- Nobody is ever going to compliment it in a coffee shop

#### My verdict

Buy the cheapest 16GB AMD configuration you can find, then upgrade the RAM yourself. Eighty dollars and fifteen minutes with a screwdriver gets you a 32GB, dual-drive-capable development machine with Windows Pro for well under $1,000 — a configuration that simply doesn’t exist as a factory option at this price.

If you want one laptop to carry you from intro data structures to your final-year capstone, this is it. Just triple-check the processor before you pay.

### 2. Dell 14 Plus (DB14250) — the best screen and the fewest surprises

Dell Pro 14 PC14250 AI Business Laptop

$949–$995 for the Core Ultra 7 258V / 32GB / 1TB configuration with the 2.5K panel

The 14 Plus is Dell’s rename of the old Inspiron 14 Plus, a decision that confused approximately everybody in 2025 and continues to confuse people searching for it today.

It’s the “nothing weird ever happens” option. Lunar Lake is x86. There’s no emulation layer, no ARM64 asterisk, no checking whether your toolchain has a native build. Every compiler, every driver, every crusty piece of departmental software that’s been limping along since 2014 — it all just runs.

#### The specs

- CPU: Intel Core Ultra 7 258V (Lunar Lake) — 8 cores, 8 threads, 4× Lion Cove P-cores to 4.8GHz plus 4× Skymont E-cores to 3.7GHz
- Graphics: Intel Arc 140V integrated
- NPU: past the 40 TOPS Copilot+ threshold, on x86
- Memory: 32GB LPDDR5X-8533 — on-package, soldered, no upgrades ever
- Storage: 1TB M.2 PCIe SSD (this part is replaceable)
- Display: 14-inch 2560×1600, 16:10, anti-glare on the non-touch configuration
- Ports: USB4 40Gbps (Thunderbolt 4 class), USB-C, USB-A, HDMI, 3.5mm
- Wireless: Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.x
- Battery: 64Wh, 4-cell
- Build: aluminium in Dell’s Ice Blue, roughly 1.51kg for the clamshell

#### The measured numbers

Battery. Laptop Mag ran their continuous web-surfing test at 150 nits and got 13 hours 25 minutes. Consumer Reports, testing a sibling configuration, logged 17 hours 45 minutes of light web browsing and 14 hours 45 minutes of 4K video playback, calling the results outstanding enough to last well beyond a typical day of mixed use.

Two different labs, two different tests, both good. For your actual workload — VS Code, browser tabs, a container ticking over, periodic builds — I’d plan on 7 to 9 hours. That’s a full timetable with room to spare.

Overall reception. Notebookcheck’s aggregate score across the 14 Plus family sits at about 76.8%, rated “good”, with strong marks for value and mobility and its weakest score in build quality. PCMag’s reviewer put it up against the 13-inch MacBook Air and the Zenbook 14 OLED and concluded it can scrap with both, especially on sale, while noting it’s heavier, not quite as fast, and could use a brighter screen. Reviewed.com called it a workhorse at a great price that gets the basics right without giving you Dell’s best trackpad.

Where it loses. Laptop Mag’s review of the 256V configuration was less kind — it fell behind the M4 MacBook Air and the Zenbook 14’s Ultra 7 258V across most benchmarks, and the reviewer criticised the display, the audio and the shallow touchpad.

Which is precisely why I’m specifying the 258V, not the 256V. Two digits, a real difference in sustained work, and Dell irritatingly hides the better configuration behind the custom-order page rather than the standard list. Go find it.

#### The Lunar Lake thing you need to understand

Lunar Lake is 8 cores and 8 threads. No hyperthreading. It’s a superb chip for battery life and for making a laptop feel instantly responsive, and a merely okay chip for long parallel compiles. A 16-thread Ryzen will finish a `make -j$(nproc)` noticeably faster.

For most CS coursework — web development, algorithms, databases, systems programming in C — you’ll never notice. If your degree leans heavily on large C++ builds, this is the wrong shape of processor and you should be looking at the ThinkPad or the LOQ.

#### Pros

- 2560×1600 in 16:10. More vertical lines of code than any 1080p machine here, and it’s genuinely sharp.
- 32GB from the factory — the most memory available in a thin-and-light at this price
- USB4 / Thunderbolt 4. One cable to a dock, or an external GPU later if you go down that road.
- Pure x86. No compatibility asterisks anywhere.
- 13h25m measured by Laptop Mag, 17h45m by Consumer Reports on light browsing
- Wi-Fi 7
- Copilot+ certified without the ARM trade-off
- Aluminium chassis that doesn’t show fingerprints

#### Cons

- Memory is soldered onto the CPU package. 32GB forever. Buy the 32GB config or don’t buy this laptop.
- 8 threads. Long parallel builds are its weakest area.
- Build quality is the lowest-scoring aspect in Notebookcheck’s aggregate
- Multiple reviewers have criticised the display quality relative to the resolution, plus the audio and the shallow touchpad
- Dell’s configuration pages are a maze — the 1600p non-touch panel requires the custom order path
- It’s the most expensive machine here. Buy it during a sale, not at list.

#### My verdict

The safe pick for anyone who values screen and battery over raw multi-core throughput. Get the 258V with 32GB and 1TB, or skip it — the 16GB version is a trap given the memory is soldered on-package. At $949 on sale it’s very good value. At $1,099 list it isn’t.

### 3. Lenovo LOQ 15 (RTX 5060) — the only real answer if you need CUDA

Lenovo LOQ 15.6″ Gaming Laptop

$799–$999 on sale for the Ryzen 7 250 / RTX 5060 / 16GB / 512GB configuration

If your degree contains the word “CUDA,” this is the only section that matters.

You cannot train models on integrated graphics. You cannot run Unreal Engine on a Radeon 780M. You cannot do meaningful local inference without VRAM. And a free Colab tier that disconnects at 3am mid-epoch is not a development environment, it’s a lottery.

The LOQ 15 is the cheapest honest way out of that corner.

#### The specs

- CPU: AMD Ryzen 7 250 — 8 cores, 16 threads, Zen 4, boost to 5.1GHz, 43W sustained / 53W burst
- Graphics: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Laptop, 8GB GDDR7, full 115W maximum graphics power, boost to 1,455MHz
- Memory: 16GB DDR5-5600 — SODIMM, two slots, upgradeable
- Storage: 512GB PCIe Gen4 — two M.2 slots, one free
- Display: 15.6-inch 1920×1080 IPS, 144Hz, anti-glare
- Ports: 3× USB-A, USB-C with 100W Power Delivery and DisplayPort 1.4, HDMI 2.1, Gigabit Ethernet, 3.5mm, barrel-plug power
- Wireless: Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 5.2
- Battery: 60Wh · Weight: 2.446kg · Webcam: 5MP

#### The 115 watts is the entire story

Notebookcheck measured the panel at around 300 nits, a 1,600:1 contrast ratio and full sRGB coverage at 144Hz — genuinely above budget-gaming-laptop average. But the screen isn’t why you buy it.

Most sub-$1,000 laptops carrying an “RTX 5060” sticker run that GPU at somewhere between 60 and 85 watts to save money on cooling and power delivery. Lenovo feeds it the full 115 watts. PCWorld confirmed the 115W figure in their teardown of the specs, and Tom’s Hardware measured the same 115W TGP on their review unit.

For you that translates directly into shorter training epochs and faster CUDA kernels. It’s the same silicon other vendors ship at two-thirds throttle.

The GPU numbers. PCWorld recorded 11,779 in 3DMark Fire Strike and 7,529 in Port Royal, the ray-traced test. Notebookcheck’s more recent review of the LOQ 15 gave the machine 81% overall, praising the two RAM slots, the dual M.2 arrangement with one bay free, and a dual-fan cooling system capable enough that the RTX 5060 in this chassis ran slightly faster than the same GPU in comparable laptops.

Thermals, measured. Tom’s Hardware ran a Metro Exodus stress test on a LOQ 15 and probed the surfaces: 108°F (42°C) between the G and H keys, 79°F (26°C) on the touchpad, and 112°F (44°C) on the underside near the fan exhaust. Internally, the CPU held 70°C and the RTX 5060 66°C. Those are good internal numbers — this thing is not thermally throttling — but 42°C under your left hand while you type is warm, and 44°C underneath means keep it off your lap during long sessions.

Battery, and it’s bad. Tom’s Hardware measured 4 hours 54 minutes on their mixed test — web browsing, OpenGL runs and video streaming at 150 nits over Wi-Fi — and called that short even by gaming laptop standards. The Acer Nitro they compared against managed over ten hours. Notebookcheck’s review listed runtimes as a con outright.

Under a real compile-plus-container workload, plan on two hours. This is a desk machine that travels, not a lecture-hall machine.

#### The stuff nobody mentions

Notebookcheck’s con list on this laptop is the most useful thing published about it, and it’s worth reproducing in spirit because none of it appears on the box:

- The RTX 5060 is sometimes barely faster than the RTX 4060 it replaces
- Idle fan noise in Performance mode is high — you’ll want to switch modes when you’re not gaming
- The SSD throttles under sustained write load. This is the one that’ll bite you when you unpack a large dataset or clone a big repository.
- Some configurations ship with 16GB in a single channel — one 16GB SODIMM in a two-slot board. Tom’s Hardware confirmed this on their unit. Single-channel memory costs you real performance on the integrated side and in memory-bound work. It also means you have a free slot, so add a matching stick and you get 32GB and dual-channel in one move. Best $65 you’ll spend.

Lenovo prices the factory upgrades at roughly $65 for 32GB and $60 for 1TB at configuration time, per PCWorld. Both are cheaper than buying the parts separately, so if you’re ordering direct, take them.

#### ⚠️ The newer model is worse. Genuinely.

Lenovo announced the LOQ 15APH11 at CES 2026 starting at $1,299. Tom’s Hardware reviewed the LOQ Essentials Gen 11 and found it pairs a decent display with a low-power RTX 5060 — their review unit retailed at $1,269.99 at Best Buy.

Newer model. Five hundred dollars more. Less GPU power.

This is one of those rare cases where the outgoing generation is flatly the better purchase. Hunt for the model code `15AHP10` with the 115W GPU, which Notebookcheck has repeatedly spotted at $799.99 on Lenovo’s own store. Check the model code in the listing, not the marketing copy above it.

#### Pros

- 8GB of VRAM and a full-power RTX 5060 under $1,000. Nothing else comes close.
- CUDA, cuDNN, PyTorch, TensorFlow — all native, no workarounds, no cloud bill
- Two RAM slots and two M.2 slots, one of each free on most configurations
- ~300 nits, ~1,600:1 contrast, full sRGB at 144Hz — a real panel, not a budget afterthought
- Internal temps of 70°C CPU / 66°C GPU under a full stress run — the cooling is genuinely competent
- Gigabit Ethernet plus three USB-A ports. Your Arduino, your external drive and your mouse, all at once.
- 100W USB-C Power Delivery, so a decent power bank or a USB-C dock will charge it
- Notebookcheck rates it 81% overall

#### Cons

- 4h54m measured battery in a 2.446kg chassis. It’s a plug-in machine.
- Heavy. Your shoulder will notice by week three.
- 42°C between the G and H keys under load, 44°C underneath
- SSD throttles under sustained writes — a real problem for dataset work
- Some configs ship single-channel 16GB; fix it with a second stick
- 1080p on a 15.6-inch panel isn’t much code real estate in 2026
- High idle fan noise in Performance mode
- Port placement puts things where your mouse hand wants to be
- It looks like a gaming laptop, because it is one

#### My verdict

Buy it if and only if you need a GPU. Machine learning, computer vision, computer graphics, game development — this is your machine and it isn’t close. Add the second RAM stick on day one.

For everyone else: you’d be carrying two and a half kilos and giving up ten hours of battery for silicon you’ll never switch on. Don’t.

### 4. HP OmniBook 5 14 — absurd battery life, one enormous caveat

HP OmniBook 5 14″ Premium Laptop

$899 for the Snapdragon X Plus X1P-42-100 / 32GB / 1TB configuration with the OLED panel

The battery numbers are ridiculous, so let’s lead with them.

- PCWorld: up to 25 hours in their rundown
- TweakTown: 28 hours 19 minutes on PCMark 10’s Applications battery benchmark, from a 59Wh cell
- Mashable: 32 hours 31 minutes in a video rundown — their reviewer noted that nothing else they’d tested had passed 25 hours

Three labs, three different tests, all extraordinary. TweakTown pointed out that most ultraportables struggle to reach 20 hours. This one treats 20 hours as a warm-up.

CNET scored it 85% and highlighted that you don’t normally find an OLED panel, 32GB of RAM and a 1TB SSD together in a sub-$1,000 laptop that weighs under three pounds and is mostly metal. Notebookcheck’s aggregate sits at 80%, praising battery, the vivid P3 OLED, keyboard ergonomics and value. PCMag handed the OmniBook family an Editors’ Choice for midrange ultraportables.

It also charges to 50% in 30 minutes from a 65W GaN brick small enough to live in a jacket pocket. PCWorld called that out specifically, and having a charger you don’t resent carrying genuinely changes how you use a laptop.

#### The specs

- CPU: Qualcomm Snapdragon X Plus X1P-42-100 (Oryon cores, ARM64)
- Graphics: Adreno integrated · NPU: on-die, Copilot+ certified
- Memory: 32GB — soldered
- Storage: 1TB SSD
- Display: 14-inch 1920×1200 OLED, P3 colour, glossy
- Ports: 2× USB-C 10Gbps with Power Delivery and DisplayPort 1.4, 1× USB-A 10Gbps, 3.5mm combo
- Battery: 59Wh · Weight: under 3lb / roughly 1.35kg
- Build: aluminium lid over a plastic chassis, “Glacier Silver”

HP also sells cheaper OmniBook 5 configurations starting at $699.99 list, which PCWorld noted have been discounted as low as $549.99 — but those drop to 16GB, 256GB and a weaker Snapdragon X chip. For CS work, the $899 32GB/1TB version is the one worth having.

#### 🚨 Read this before you buy anything

This laptop runs Windows on ARM. Every generic student-laptop roundup will sell you this machine without mentioning any of what follows.

Runs natively, and runs well:

- VS Code (native ARM64 build), Visual Studio 2022
- Python, Node.js, Go, Rust — all ship ARM64 Windows builds
- Git, Windows Terminal, WSL2 running ARM64 Linux distributions
- Docker Desktop — but it runs ARM64 container images
- Chrome, Firefox, Edge, the Office suite

Runs under emulation — slower, sometimes strange:

- Most x86-64 desktop applications
- Older IDEs and departmental tooling without ARM builds

Doesn’t work, or fights you the whole way:

- x86-64 Docker images. A large slice of Docker Hub is amd64-only. A Compose file with `platform: linux/amd64` in it will either fail outright or crawl under QEMU translation.
- Android Studio’s x86 emulator system images
- CUDA. Obviously.
- Certain VPN clients, endpoint security agents and lab drivers your department mandates
- Kernel-level anti-cheat, if you were hoping to unwind with games

TweakTown’s verdict was pointed: worth investigating if you don’t need it to do much beyond Office and browser-based work, and they noted ARM compatibility is improving but isn’t there yet. That’s an accurate summary.

Here’s the test I’d actually run. Open your course syllabi. If you see “Docker,” “VirtualBox,” “Android Studio,” or a named commercial toolchain, buy something x86. If your work is web development, JavaScript, Python, cloud-first tooling and a lot of note-taking, this machine will change your relationship with the campus outlet situation permanently.

#### Pros

- 25 to 32 hours measured across three independent labs. Nothing else on this list is in the same postcode.
- 32GB, 1TB and an OLED panel under $1,000 is an absurd amount of hardware for the money
- Vivid 1920×1200 P3 OLED in 16:10
- Under three pounds, and the 65W GaN charger is genuinely pocketable
- 50% charge in half an hour
- Keyboard and trackpad praised across essentially every review
- Silent under normal load — no fan noise in a quiet library
- CNET 85%, Notebookcheck aggregate 80%, PCMag Editors’ Choice

#### Cons

- ARM64. See above. This is the entire risk and it’s not a small one.
- Soldered 32GB
- The X1P-42-100 is among the least powerful Snapdragon X Plus parts. PCWorld put it plainly: good for battery life, a negative for performance.
- Glossy OLED reflects everything behind you
- TechRadar noted it runs a bit warm and that build quality could be better; Notebookcheck flags the limited port selection
- Weak graphics — casual photo editing is roughly the ceiling
- Notebookcheck also flags pricing confusion across retailers; check exactly which configuration you’re buying
- OLED panels use PWM dimming, which bothers some people’s eyes over long sessions. If you’re sensitive to flicker, try one in a shop first.

#### My verdict

Brilliant for the right CS student, quietly frustrating for the wrong one. Web development, cloud-native work, heavy note-taking, long days nowhere near a plug — outstanding, and the battery genuinely changes your habits. Systems programming, machine learning, or anything with a mandated x86 toolchain —

## What $1,000 Buys in 2026

The biggest story in laptops this year isn’t a new chip. It’s memory. AI data centers are absorbing huge amounts of the world’s RAM supply, so laptop makers are raising prices, cutting specs, or both.

Global PC shipments fell for the first time in two years in the second quarter of 2026, according to our breakdown of the data. Asus was the only Windows brand to grow, while Apple’s MacBook shipments rose 13%, largely thanks to the MacBook Neo.

Here’s what that means for you. At $700, most laptops ship with 8GB of RAM. At $1,000, you can get 16GB or even 32GB. We think that jump is the single best reason to spend more. More memory means you can keep more apps and browser tabs open without slowdowns, and it helps your laptop stay usable for five years instead of three.

After comparing these laptops, our biggest takeaway is that the “AI PC” label means very little for most buyers. Acer’s AI features felt underdeveloped to reviewers, and most useful AI tools, like ChatGPT or Gemini, run in the cloud anyway.

What does matter is memory, battery life, and screen quality, in that order. Here’s the quick version:

## FAQs

### Is an Intel, AMD, or Snapdragon chip better for a laptop under $1,000? 

It depends on your priority. Snapdragon chips usually offer the longest battery life, but some older apps and games don’t run as smoothly. Intel’s Lunar Lake and AMD’s Ryzen AI chips balance battery life with broad software support. For gaming, you want an AMD or Intel chip paired with an Nvidia graphics card.

### Should I buy a laptop with an AI chip (NPU)? 

An NPU (neural processing unit) is a part of the chip designed for AI tasks like background blur on video calls. It’s nice to have, but it shouldn’t decide your purchase. Most popular AI tools run in the cloud, so RAM, battery life, and screen quality matter much more today.

### Is 512GB of storage enough, or do I need 1TB? 

For most people, 512GB is enough if you store photos and videos in the cloud. Gamers and video editors should aim for 1TB, since modern games can take up over 100GB each. If you pick a 512GB laptop, a portable SSD is an affordable way to add space later.

### Are open-box or refurbished laptops a good way to stretch $1,000? 

Yes, when bought from the manufacturer or a major retailer with a warranty. You can often get a higher-spec model, like 32GB of RAM, for the price of a new 16GB laptop. Check the return window, battery health, and warranty length before you buy.

### Will laptop prices drop in 2027? 

Probably not much. IDC doesn’t expect relief from the memory shortage before the end of 2027. The memory squeeze is hitting every device, as our breakdown of the global RAM shortage behind rising prices shows. Holiday sales on existing stock are your best bet for a discount.
